title: The Five Mightiest Powers
author: The Essence of Practice
excerpt: For practice to become a way of life, one should cultivate the five powers. If we possess these five powers, bodhicitta will naturally arise in the mind.

inline.s: Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche
(Excerpted from The Courage to Awaken)
For practice to become a way of life, one should cultivate the five powers. If we possess these five powers, bodhicitta will naturally arise in the mind.
These five powers are: the power of determination, the power of familiarity, the power of virtuous causes, the power of confession, and the power of aspiration.
1. The Power of Determination

For example, we resolve that within this month, or this year, or until death, or until enlightenment, we will never abandon bodhicitta; even when harmed by others, we will not give way to anger. We must continually strengthen this firm determination.
2. The Power of Familiarity
At first, meditation is difficult. But if we persevere, it will become easier and easier. As the saying goes: “There is nothing one cannot grow accustomed to.”
There was once a very miserly man who could not give anything away. He went to see the Buddha and said: “I simply cannot practice generosity. What should I do?”

The Buddha replied: “Imagine that your right hand is you and your left hand is a poor, wretched person. Take some old food you dislike or do not need from your right hand and give it to your left hand, and try to grow accustomed to doing this. Keep doing it until you are no longer stingy.”

The man began to practice, but at first he was so miserly that he could give his left hand only a tiny bit of food he disliked or had left over. Gradually he grew accustomed to it, until one day he felt he was not so stingy anymore, and he went to report to the Buddha again: “Now when I pass food from my right hand to my left, my mind is not so reluctant.” The Buddha replied: “Still regard your right hand as yourself, and take some gold, silk, or fine garments to give to your left hand, which you imagine to be a beggar, and see whether you can give generously without any thought of greed.” The man strove to do this, and once the habit was formed, he went to see the Buddha again. The Buddha said: “Now you can become a benefactor of merit. You have been freed from clinging, and you can give food and clothing to those in need.”

The man was freed from his miserliness and helped many beggars and the poor. He practiced step by step, until at last his generosity was steady and unshakable. He came to understand that excessive thrift and clinging to wealth are meaningless. He later became a monk and attained the state of an arhat. Through diligent practice, we too can accomplish the two kinds of bodhicitta.

[The two kinds of bodhicitta] relative bodhicitta and ultimate bodhicitta. [Relative bodhicitta] One who arouses relative bodhicitta, though not yet enlightened, has generated in the heart the great vow: “I must save all sentient beings; in order to save all sentient beings, I must attain Buddhahood.” [Ultimate bodhicitta] After arousing relative bodhicitta, one practices the various bodhisattva deeds and at last awakens, realizing emptiness and seeing the true nature of all phenomena; the bodhicitta aroused at that moment is called ultimate bodhicitta.
3. The Power of Virtuous Causes

This is the accumulation of merit. When we go to a temple and perform prostrations and make offerings before the sacred objects, we should pray in our hearts: “May the two kinds of bodhicitta arise in my mind. May my mind be peaceful and free of anger toward those who harm me. May I be freed from the one-sided clinging I feel toward my family and friends.” Praying in this way without ceasing, through the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, we will accomplish these merits.
4. The Power of Confession

By thinking carefully, we can see that all the suffering and affliction we undergo in this life are calamities created by self-clinging; self-clinging is the root of all evil. The moment it arises, even for an instant, we should at once apply the antidote, just as when we are ill a physician gives us a remedy for the illness. As the saying goes: “Strike the pig on the nose; clean the oil lamp while it is still warm.” When an angry wild boar charges at us, a blow to its nose with a stick will make it turn and flee at once, unable to bear the pain. When the oil lamp is cleaned before it has cooled, it is easily wiped clean. Likewise, if we apply the medicine before self-clinging has gathered strength, we will not be swayed by it.
5. The Power of Aspiration

Whenever we complete some virtuous deed, we should pray: “From now until awakening, may I never abandon the two kinds of bodhicitta. Whatever conflicts and afflictions I encounter, may I be able to use them as stepping-stones on the path.” Praying in this way, make offerings to the guru, the Three Jewels, and the Dharma protectors, and request their assistance.

These five powers contain all the Dharma, condensed into the single syllable “hūṃ (hōng).” This means that all the profound and complex teachings on mind training are contained within these five powers. Therefore, we should practice these five powers ardently. The Buddha did so in one of his lifetimes, in which he was a hermit of the royal family — the Ascetic Kshantivadin.

The story goes like this: the Ascetic Kshantivadin went into the forest to practice austerities. Later, his younger brother inherited the throne. One day this brother, the king, went on a long journey and stopped to rest in a place in the forest, where he fell asleep. Meanwhile, the queen, the ministers, and the guards left him and went to see the Ascetic Kshantivadin, whom they had known before, to seek his teaching. When the king awoke and found himself alone, he thought the queen, the ministers, and the guards had abandoned him. Enraged, he rose and searched for them, and found them gathered around a hermit. He did not know that this sage was giving them a teaching; instead he thought the hermit was leading the queen and ministers astray.
The king shouted: “Who are you?” Because he had been very young when his brother had left the world, he did not recognize him.
The brother said: “I am the Ascetic Kshantivadin.”
The king said: “Then I shall see whether you deserve such a name. Let me see how much forbearance you can bear.” As he spoke, he cut off the hermit's right hand. “Can you bear it?” he said.
The hermit replied: “Yes.”
The king then cut off the hermit's left hand and said: “Are you still the Ascetic Kshantivadin? Can you still bear it?”
The king then cut off the hermit's head and said: “Can you still bear it?”

The king had cut off the hermit's hands and head, yet the wounds did not bleed; instead a white, milk-like liquid flowed out. The king calmed down and thought that this might not be an ordinary person. He asked his attendants who the hermit was. They told him: “He is your brother, the Ascetic Kshantivadin. He gave up the kingdom long ago and went into the forest to practice.” Hearing this, the king was overcome with remorse and began to weep. Because the Ascetic Kshantivadin was a bodhisattva, even with his head cut off he could still speak. He said: “As you asked questions, you cut off my head and hands. In a future life, after I have attained Buddhahood, when you ask me questions, may I likewise cut off your delusion.”
In fact, the Ascetic Kshantivadin was none other than the later Śākyamuni Buddha.
After Śākyamuni Buddha attained enlightenment, his first five disciples (one of whom was the younger brother of the Ascetic Kshantivadin of old) asked him: “What is samsara?”
The Buddha said: “Samsara is in essence suffering.”
Then they asked: “Where does suffering come from?”
The Buddha said: “Suffering comes from afflictive emotions.”
They asked again: “How do we eliminate the cause of suffering?”
The Buddha said: “You must follow the path.”
They asked further: “What is the benefit of following the path?”
The Buddha said: “After following the path, all karma and afflictions will cease.” Through this teaching, the five disciples attained the state of arhats.

Although the Ascetic Kshantivadin's head was cut off in anger, through his powerful aspiration for enlightenment he was able to transform the evil karma, so that the king became his disciple in a future life. From this story we can see why the Dharma teaches that we must make aspirations.
Next, let us discuss the teaching on death in the Buddhist tradition. According to the mind-training instructions, the practice of transference of consciousness is as the tantra says:
The Mahayana instruction on death: rely on the five powers yourself.
As stated earlier, these five powers are: the power of virtuous causes, the power of aspiration, the power of confession, the power of determination, and the power of familiarity.
1. The Power of Virtuous Causes

As practitioners, when we know we are stricken with a terminal illness, that our life cannot be prolonged, and that we are about to die, we should offer all our possessions to the guru and the Three Jewels, and give to those most in need and to the most meritorious recipients. At the same time, we should finish all unfinished business, holding no clinging or resentment toward anyone or anything.
2. The Power of Aspiration

Make the seven-branch offering to the guru and the Three Jewels, and pray thus: “May I be free from fear in the bardo. In all my future lives, may I receive the blessings to practice the two kinds of bodhicitta. May the victorious ones, and especially the guru who bestowed the mind-training teachings and taught me to practice bodhicitta, grant me their blessings.” Pray in this way without ceasing, deeply trusting that the guru will surely watch over us.
[Seven-branch offering]
that is,

the seven-branch offering: 1. the branch of prostrations; 2. the branch of offerings; 3. the branch of confession; 4. the branch of rejoicing; 5. the branch of requesting the turning of the Dharma wheel; 6. the branch of beseeching the Buddhas not to enter nirvana; 7. the branch of dedication. Through the practice of the seven-branch offering, one can eliminate karmic obstructions and perfect the accumulations. This offering is the most sublime way to accumulate merit and wisdom, the swiftest way to attain accomplishment in this very life, and the essential gateway to the state of the noble ones.
[Bardo]
the bardo body,

also called the intermediate state, which is the subtle, material, apparitional body that sustains life after death but before rebirth; this apparitional body is the bardo body. During the first forty-nine days, this bardo body undergoes one death and rebirth every seven days, passing through seven deaths and rebirths while awaiting the arrangement of karmic conditions before taking rebirth.
3. The Power of Confession

We should remember that self-clinging has brought us pain; even now we still hope to prolong our life, clinging to the body as something precious, worrying about how our wealth might be used up: all of this still causes much suffering. If, at this point, we cannot free ourselves from such clinging, we will never find peace. Let go of your body, regard it as mud and stone, and think that it is not worth clinging to. We suffer precisely because we cling to the body. One need only look! Outside, the body is skin; inside, it is filled with flesh, blood, bones, and all manner of repulsive matter. The body is merely a bag full of dust; there is no need to identify it as oneself. Let them take it and burn it, or give it to the birds and dogs to eat! Thinking in this way, one can dispel self-clinging.
4. The Power of Determination

Remind yourself that when passing through the bardo, if you can meditate on the sublime bodhicitta — which is in fact the essence of the practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas — you will not fall into the three lower realms. Form a strong determination to practice bodhicitta continually, and you can protect yourself from the terrors of the bardo.
5. The Power of Familiarity

We should continually review the techniques described above: how to practice the two kinds of bodhicitta, how to practice exchanging self and others, and how to arouse compassion toward those who bear us ill will. In daily life, keep the mind-training methods in mind at all times. In this way
when death comes and we endure much pain, we will have the ability to put them to use.

At the moment of death, you should do this: as the Buddha lay at his passing, lie on your right side with your head resting on your right hand. Block the right nostril with the little finger of your right hand and breathe through the left nostril. Meditate on loving-kindness, wishing that all beings, vast as space, may obtain happiness; then meditate on compassion, wishing that all beings may be freed from every suffering. As you breathe out, give all your happiness, comfort, and wealth to all suffering beings. As you breathe in, draw into yourself all beings' sickness, evil, negative emotions, and obstacles.

Afterward, you should contemplate that samsara and nirvana themselves are like dreams and illusions, or like a magician's tricks, and that all things lack inherent existence. Whether here or in the bardo, everything is but the awareness of mind; nothing truly exists, and there is no cause for fear. Strive to sustain this conviction, with no clinging in the mind.

Once, an old woman and her daughter were swept away by a river. The old woman thought: “So long as my daughter is saved, I do not mind drowning myself!” The daughter thought: “What does it matter if I die? So long as my mother is safe!” In the end both died, but because their final wishes were so full of love, they were reborn in the god realm. We should always hold such loving thoughts. When death comes, we should meditate on the two kinds of bodhicitta in turn.
There are many renowned teachings on how to transfer consciousness at the moment of death, but none is more supreme, more wondrous, or more inconceivable than this one.
